questions.question_text: A squash player wins each rally independently with probability $0.6$. A game lasts $7$ rallies. Find the probability that she wins exactly $5$ of them, correct to four decimal places.

options.why: Used $r=4$ instead of $r=5$ successes.
Swapped $p$ and $1-p$, using $0.4$ as the probability of winning a rally.
Left out the factor ${}^{7}C_{5}$, so only one arrangement was counted.

questions.question_text: A high jumper clears the opening height on each of her attempts independently with probability $0.15$ when the bar is raised to a record height. She makes $10$ such attempts over a season. Find the probability that she clears it exactly twice, correct to four decimal places.

options.why: Used $r=3$ instead of $r=2$ successes.
Used $r=1$ instead of $r=2$ successes.
Found $P(X \le 2)$ rather than the single term $P(X=2)$.

questions.question_text: A cricketer takes a catch cleanly on each of $50$ chances independently with probability $0.72$. Let $X$ be the number of clean catches. Find $\text{Var}(X)$.

options.why: Gave the mean $np$ instead of the variance $np(1-p)$.
Gave the standard deviation $\sqrt{np(1-p)}$ instead of the variance.
Found $n(1-p)$, leaving the factor $p$ out of the variance.

questions.question_text: A volleyball server lands each serve independently with probability $0.45$. She serves $20$ times in a match. Find the standard deviation of the number of serves she lands, correct to two decimal places.

options.why: Gave the variance $np(1-p)$ without taking the square root.
Gave the mean $np$ instead of the standard deviation.
Used $n\sqrt{p(1-p)}$, multiplying the Bernoulli standard deviation by $n$ instead of by $\sqrt{n}$.

questions.question_text: The number of races a sprinter wins in a season is $X \sim \text{Bin}(n,p)$, with $E(X) = 14$ and $\text{Var}(X) = 8.4$. Find $n$.

options.why: Took $\frac{\text{Var}(X)}{E(X)}$ to be $p$ rather than $1-p$, giving $p=0.6$.
Divided the variance by $p$ instead of dividing the mean by $p$.
Read the mean $E(X)$ itself as the number of trials.

questions.question_text: A footballer scores from each set piece independently with probability $0.25$. Find the smallest number of set pieces she must take for the probability of scoring from at least one to exceed $0.95$.

options.why: Rounded $10.41$ down instead of up, giving a probability still below $0.95$.
Solved for a probability above $0.99$ rather than above $0.95$.
Solved $(0.25)^{n} < 0.05$, using $p$ in place of $1-p$ in the complement.

questions.solution_text:
Success: the set piece is scored.
$1 - (0.75)^{n} > 0.95$
$(0.75)^{n} < 0.05$
$n\log 0.75 < \log 0.05$
$n > \frac{\log 0.05}{\log 0.75}$
$n > 10.41\ldots$
She must take $11$ set pieces.

questions.question_text: A water polo team plays $24$ matches and wins each independently with probability $0.25$. Find the expected number of matches the team wins.

options.why: Used $1-p$, giving the expected number of matches lost.
Found the variance $np(1-p)$ instead of the mean $np$.
Divided $24$ by $0.25$ instead of multiplying.

questions.question_text: Player P takes $8$ shots and scores each independently with probability $0.3$. Player Q takes $6$ shots and scores each independently with probability $0.4$. Which player is more likely to score exactly $2$ shots?

options.text: Player P, because $8$ shots give more chances of scoring exactly $2$ than $6$ shots do.
options.why: Compared the number of trials instead of evaluating both probabilities.

options.text: Player P, because a lower probability of scoring makes a small number of successes more likely.
